part_title: Cost Explorer: Spend Analysis, Resource Investigation, Savings Plans and Forecasts

scenes.title: Cost Explorer Report Anatomy
scenes.narration: The diagram breaks down a Cost Explorer report into the choices that determine what the chart means. First set a time range and granularity: daily or monthly, with hourly detail only where currently supported and enabled. Next choose the metric. Unblended cost represents charges under its billing treatment, while amortized cost spreads eligible up-front commitments over the relevant period; net metrics may reflect applicable discounts. Those views answer different questions, so don't mix them casually in a trend comparison. Apply filters for service, linked account, tag or cost category and choose a group-by dimension. The sample report compares EC2, S3, RDS and Lambda cost and usage units. A request count is not comparable to compute hours, so examine the metric and units together. Cost Explorer is based on billing data and is not real-time telemetry. Recent costs can arrive late, and the level of supported hourly or resource granularity depends on configuration and service. Record the exact filters and cost metric when sharing results so someone else can reproduce the conclusion.

scenes.title: Monthly Cost Comparison
scenes.narration: This slide compares one month's spend with the next rather than presenting a raw invoice. Read the table by service. EC2 rises from one hundred to one hundred twenty dollars, a twenty-dollar or twenty-percent increase. S3 stays unchanged. Bedrock rises substantially and accounts for eighty dollars of the one-hundred-dollar total increase. Overall monthly cost moves from two hundred to three hundred dollars, a fifty-percent rise. These numbers are illustrative and the important lesson is attribution. A percentage change alone can be misleading: a service can show a huge percentage increase from a tiny baseline, while another service contributes more absolute dollars. Look at both amounts and relative percentages. For a GenAI product, Bedrock cost might increase because of request volume, token length, model selection or retries. Before declaring waste, normalise cost by useful work, such as cost per answered request, and compare usage with user growth and quality metrics. The first question is which service drove the change; the next is whether it reflects healthy adoption or an avoidable regression.

scenes.title: Hourly and Resource-Level Cost Investigation
scenes.narration: The workflow here turns a broad cost spike into a specific investigation. First enable the detailed billing data that the organisation actually needs, including supported resource identifiers. Then narrow the report to one service, Region, usage type and linked account before drilling down. In the example, an hourly cost line is accompanied by instance IDs, instance families, usage hours and dollar charges. This allows an investigator to distinguish greater usage from a more expensive unit rate or a change in instance type. Be careful about the apparent completeness of the sample table: not every AWS service exposes every resource-level billing identifier and some views require additional setup or have different retention limits. Hourly granularity is also not a substitute for CloudWatch's near-real-time operational metrics. For inference fleets, correlate the billing spike with Auto Scaling activity, GPU utilisation, request throughput and deployment changes. Enable resource-specific cost data judiciously, considering access controls and any additional charges. A precise filter sequence makes the investigation repeatable and reduces the chance of blaming the wrong resource.

scenes.title: Savings Plans Decision
scenes.narration: This decision diagram starts with a question: how stable is your eligible compute spending? A Savings Plan trades a commitment to a specified hourly spend over a term for discounted usage that qualifies under the selected plan. The example contrasts ten thousand dollars in On-Demand spend with a lower illustrative amount after commitment. It is not a universal thirty-percent discount. Compute Savings Plans offer broader flexibility across qualifying compute, while EC2 Instance Savings Plans focus on specified EC2 instance attributes and may offer a different discount level. Examine the two measurements at the bottom. Utilisation asks what portion of the committed amount was actually consumed by qualifying usage; coverage asks what portion of eligible compute usage received a benefit. A large unused commitment can erase expected savings. Review recommendations, existing commitments, seasonality and future architecture changes before committing. Be particularly careful with AI costs: a compute plan does not automatically discount Bedrock model inference or all external API spending. Base the decision on eligible usage and realistic growth, not just the headline discount.

scenes.title: Cost Forecasting
scenes.narration: This graph separates observed monthly charges from projected future costs and an uncertainty band. Historical spend supplies the evidence for a forecast, and the predicted range widens as the horizon extends because future demand is less certain. A forecast is not a guarantee, a hard limit or a purchase recommendation. It can also be unavailable or unreliable when there is insufficient history or recent spending changes sharply. Follow the three steps at the bottom: inspect historical costs, interpret the range of plausible future spend, and compare the projection with the budget and business plan. If a new GenAI model, GPU fleet or retrieval service launches next month, the historical trend alone may not incorporate that architectural change. Adjust the planning assumptions, monitor actuals and reforecast once new usage appears. Compare cost per successful request alongside absolute spend so increasing adoption isn't mistaken for poor efficiency. Forecasting is most useful as an input into decisions about budgets, capacity and optimisation rather than an oracle.
